name: ActiveDirectory Module - Import
description: Imports the built-in Microsoft ActiveDirectory PowerShell module. Available on domain-joined Windows hosts with RSAT tools or on Domain Controllers by default. Provides Get-AD* cmdlets for authoritative AD enumeration - uses LDAP under the hood but wraps it cleanly. More 'legitimate-looking' than PowerView but requires the module to be installed.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== WHEN THE MODULE IS AVAILABLE ===
  - All Domain Controllers (installed by default)
  - Windows hosts with RSAT (Remote Server Administration Tools) installed
  - If not installed: Install-WindowsFeature RSAT-AD-PowerShell (server)
  - Or: Get-WindowsCapability -Online | Where Name -like 'Rsat.ActiveDirectory*' | Add-WindowsCapability -Online

=== ACTIVEDIRECTORY MODULE vs POWERVIEW ===
  AD Module (Microsoft):
    + Legitimate, signed, built-in - low detection risk
    + Consistent, well-documented cmdlets
    - Requires RSAT/installation on client systems
    - Less flexible than PowerView for attack-oriented tasks

  PowerView (offensive):
    + No installation required - drop-and-run .ps1
    + Richer output, better for attack enumeration (ACLs, trusts, shares)
    - May trigger AV/AMSI
    - Deprecated/unmaintained (use SharpView for updated version)

=== KEY CMDLETS AFTER IMPORT ===
  Get-ADDomain                    → domain info, SIDs, functional levels
  Get-ADUser -Filter *            → all users
  Get-ADGroup -Filter *           → all groups  
  Get-ADComputer -Filter *        → all computers
  Get-ADGroupMember 'Domain Admins' → group membership
  Get-ADTrust -Filter *           → trust relationships
  Get-ADUser -Filter {ServicePrincipalName -ne '$null'} → Kerberoastable users

=== IMPORT FROM CUSTOM PATH ===
If module is not in PSModulePath:
  Import-Module C:\path\to\Microsoft.ActiveDirectory.Management.dll
Or using the full module path:
  Import-Module C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\Modules\ActiveDirectory\ActiveDirectory.psd1

references.title: HTB Academy - Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks

defense.why_it_works: Imports the Microsoft ActiveDirectory PowerShell module (or its DLL) to run native AD cmdlets for enumeration without external tools.
defense.prerequisites: A domain-joined or credentialed Windows host with the AD module (or its DLL) available.
defense.impact: Native, trusted AD cmdlets ready for stealthy enumeration.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1059.001] PowerShell module import / script-block logging (4104); loading of the AD module DLL.
defense.artifacts: Module import in PowerShell logs; the ActiveDirectory module loaded.
defense.splunk_spl:
index=wineventlog EventCode=4104 (ScriptBlockText=\"*Import-Module ActiveDirectory*\" OR ScriptBlockText=\"*addsadministration*\")
| table _time, Computer, User, ScriptBlockText
defense.sentinel_kql:
DeviceEvents
| where ActionType == "PowerShellCommand"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Import-Module ActiveDirectory", "addsadministration")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ProcessCommandLine
| sort by Timestamp desc
defense.prevention: Script-block + module logging; constrained language mode; the module itself is legitimate, so detection is behavioural.
defense.evasion: The AD module is a signed Microsoft tool, so its cmdlets blend with admin activity better than third-party tools.
defense.misconfiguration: Active Directory's default read ACL allows any authenticated domain user to enumerate nearly the entire directory: all user accounts, groups, SPNs, computer objects, trust relationships, and many sensitive attributes. There is no built-in 'need to know' principle on LDAP reads. BloodHound, PowerView, and ldapsearch all exploit these open default ACLs to map attack paths.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# AD default permissions - authenticated users can read:
# All user objects: sAMAccountName, userPrincipalName, memberOf, servicePrincipalName
# All computer objects: DNS names, OS versions, operating system attributes
# All group memberships, GPOs, OU structure, domain trusts

# Verify with any low-priv account:
Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties *  # returns all users + attributes
Get-ADGroup -Filter * | Get-ADGroupMember  # all group memberships
defense.secure_config:
# 1. Enable AD Recycle Bin + Protected Users group
# 2. Audit and tighten ACLs on sensitive attributes:
#    msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo, adminCount, memberOf for privileged groups

# 3. Disable SMB null sessions + restrict LDAP anonymous binds (see smb/ldap cards)

# 4. Detect enumeration via volume:
# Sysmon Event 3 (network connection) from non-DC to DC on port 389/636
# Event 4661 - access to SAM objects (high-volume; baseline first)
# Microsoft Defender for Identity: 'Account Enumeration Reconnaissance' alert

# 5. Deploy Honey accounts/objects:
# Fake high-priv account (no real access) - any LDAP query for it = attacker
# BloodHound run from non-DC = detectable via DC LDAP traffic volume

# 6. Tiered administration: Tier 0 DCs, Tier 1 servers, Tier 2 workstations
#    Each tier can only query its own tier's objects

validation.success_criteria: At least one behavioral detection fires within 60 seconds of attack execution
response_steps: Correlate alert with source host, user account, and timestamp
Review PowerShell Script Block / Module Logs, Windows Security Event Log for surrounding context (5 min before/after)
Verify whether the activity matches known administrative baselines or change windows
If confirmed malicious, isolate the host and escalate to incident response

variations.label: Import the DLL directly (no RSAT install)
variations.description: Loads the Active Directory PowerShell module for AD enumeration and management. The DLL can be imported directly without RSAT installation on the target, making it usable from a compromised workstation.

explain:
Loads Microsoft's ActiveDirectory PowerShell module:
  Import-Module ActiveDirectory   bring the Get-AD* cmdlets into the session
Requires RSAT (or runs by default on a DC); once loaded you get authoritative, LDAP-backed enumeration cmdlets. Verify with 'Get-Module -Name ActiveDirectory'.
